claims.claim: Muhammad lived c. 570-632 CE, and Islamic civilization originated in early-seventh-century Arabia around Mecca and Medina.
Arab-Muslim armies expanded rapidly beginning around 634, taking much of the Byzantine and Sasanian territory by the 650s and reaching from Iberia to Central Asia within roughly a century.
The first four caliphs (Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali) ruled 632-661 and are called the Rashidun ('rightly guided').
The Umayyad dynasty established Islam's first hereditary dynasty in 661, moved the capital from Medina to Damascus, and ruled until 750.
The Abbasids took power in 750 and founded a new capital, Baghdad, in central Iraq (begun 762); they added little territory but oversaw the transmission and growth of knowledge.
The Abbasid (Greco-Arabic) translation movement rendered works of Aristotle, Galen, Ptolemy, and others into Arabic; Chinese papermaking made books cheaper.

Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780-c. 850) was a scholar at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad under al-Ma'mun; the word 'algebra' derives from the title of his treatise Al-jabr wa'l-muqabala, and the word 'algorithm' derives from a Latin rendering of his name.
Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980-1037) wrote the Canon of Medicine, one of the most influential medical texts, used as a standard reference in Europe for centuries.

Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, 965-1040) wrote the Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir), gave the first correct account of vision, and insisted on experiment over assumption, an early form of scientific method; it was translated into Latin in 1270.

Al-Andalus began with the Muslim conquest of Iberia in 711; the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba was founded in 756 and became the Caliphate of Córdoba (929-1031); Muslim political rule in Iberia ended in 1492 with the fall of Granada.
Knowledge preserved and extended in the Islamic world passed into Europe largely through Latin translations of Arabic works (e.g., at Toledo), helping to seed the European Renaissance.

The Sunni/Shia distinction originates in the seventh-century dispute over rightful succession after Muhammad; Sunnis accepted the line of caliphs beginning with Abu Bakr, while Shia held leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact span of the 'Islamic Golden Age.'
positions: Commonly dated roughly 8th to 13th century, sometimes extended to the 14th
Some accounts date its end to the 1258 Mongol sack of Baghdad specifically
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as an approximate convention ('roughly the eighth to the thirteenth century') rather than a fixed span, consistent with the caution against stating conventional period boundaries as exact.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Founding date attributed to the House of Wisdom.
positions: Associated with Harun al-Rashid and especially al-Ma'mun (r. 813-833)
Sometimes given a specific founding of 830 CE under al-Ma'mun
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson associates the House of Wisdom with al-Ma'mun and Abbasid Baghdad without asserting a single disputed founding year.

sourceRecords.title: World History Volume 1, to 1500 — Chapter 11: The Rise of Islam and the Caliphates (11.2 The Arab-Islamic Conquests and the First Islamic States; 11.3 Islamization and Religious Rule under Islam)
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19 (sections 11.2 and 11.3). Confirms: Muhammad died 632; Rashidun caliphs (Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali) ruled 632-661; conquests from 634, much Byzantine/Sasanian territory taken by the 650s; Umayyads established the first hereditary dynasty in 661, moved the capital to Damascus, ended 750; Abbasids took power 750 and founded Baghdad on the Tigris; the Greco-Arabic translation movement (Aristotle, Galen, Ptolemy) and cheaper books via Chinese papermaking. Used for narrative and dates; prose original.

sourceRecords.title: Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) - MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive
sourceRecords.provider: University of St Andrews (School of Mathematics and Statistics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. Confirms Ibn al-Haytham born 965 (Basra), died 1040 (Cairo); the seven-volume Kitab al-Manazir (Book of Optics), translated into Latin in 1270 as Opticae thesaurus; his correct explanation of vision and his insistence on experimental evidence over abstract theory. Prose original.

sourceRecords.title: Al-Andalus - World History Encyclopedia
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. Confirms the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba (756-929) becoming the Caliphate of Córdoba (929-1031); Abd al-Rahman I (r. 756-788); a tenth-century golden age of Muslim Spain; and the Reconquista (11th-13th c.). The 711 conquest date and the 1492 fall of Granada were verified via corroborating search sources (Wikipedia, Britannica summaries); this entry supports the emirate/caliphate spans and the transmission context. Prose original.
